title: Session Thrash Lab — long context & high TPS stress demo
summary: Redwood AE+SE ran a technical lab showing long-context stability and streaming backpressure behavior under high TPS. Discussed buffering, KV cache eviction strategies, timeouts, and Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs. Agreed pilot: Dedicated trial with 2-week benchmarking, provide tuning guide and latency matrix.
topics: KV cache eviction and prefix caching
Dedicated vs Hosted for sustained high TPS
meeting_header: Date: 2025-11-13 15:00 PST | Duration: 78 mins | Redwood: Lara Chen, Marcus Nguyen | Atlas: Priya Desai, Omar Khalid, Sofia Morales
transcript:
[00:00] Lara (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. We setup this as a lab rather than a straight slide demo — want to push a few weird combos, long histories plus bursts. Marcus will drive the test harness.
[00:12] Priya (Atlas): Thanks Lara. Our main thing: we have chatbots that keep up to 80k token histories for some enterprise workflows, and peak TPS during Black Friday is a concern. We wanna see how you handle history trimming + streaming.
[00:28] Marcus (Redwood-SE): Cool. Quick agenda — 1) reproduce long-context generation with 60–80k token prefixes, 2) subject to high TPS bursts 200–500 TPS sustained, and 3) observe streaming backpressure and timeouts on long tails. I'll start the harness in a minute.
[00:45] Omar (Atlas): Just to be clear — our clients require sub-300ms initial token latency for search-autocomplete like flows, but we're okay if tail tokens during super-long sessions hit higher numbers.
[00:58] Lara (Redwood): Good constraint. We'll surface both p50 and p99 and show how routing and auto-fallbacks work. Also we'll toggle Dedicated pool later so you can see tradeoffs.
[01:12] Marcus: Kicking off test run one now. Note: the harness uses realistic user histories we pulled from Atlas sandbox (anonymized). We'll simulate mixed lengths — 8k, 32k, 64k and a set with 80k tokens. Streaming enabled, chunk size 512.
[01:34] [system noise, background typing] 
[01:50] Marcus: First observation — with Hosted default model profile we see good single-request throughput but at 64k+ histories we start to hit KV cache misses and kernel paths fall back to slower attention kernels, so p50 for first token jumps to ~420ms.
[02:06] Priya: When you say KV cache misses, you mean the prefix isn't in the cache so you recompute a lot? Can you explain the tradeoffs there.
[02:16] Marcus: Yeah. Our runtime tries to cache common prefix key/values to avoid reencoding long context every request. When the prefix is unusual or very large, the cache evicts older entries to make room. That causes cold recompute which is heavier, and when multiple such cold requests come in concurrently we see throughput erosion.
[02:36] Sofia: Is eviction LRU? Can we pin prefixes for specific accounts?
[02:41] Marcus: Currently eviction is workload-aware LRU with weighting by size. For Dedicated we support pinning hot prefixes to reserved memory — practical for VIP accounts. For Hosted, you can request reserved slots if you hit a committed tier.
[02:58] Omar: Okay run two please, this time start a 500 TPS burst for 30s after steady state.
[03:05] Marcus: Running. Also enabling streaming flush windows tighter to mimic low-latency clients.
[03:22] [~30s later] 
[03:25] Marcus: Observing immediate queueing on the serving nodes — our admission control kicks in and we throttle lower-priority routes. For the high-priority VIP route we see graceful fallback to a smaller model variant to preserve throughput, but streaming gets chunkier — clients receive initial tokens on time but later chunks arrive in bursts.
[03:45] Priya: So clients will see intermittent pauses in the stream? How bad is that for UX?
[03:52] Lara: It depends on your client. We recommend client-side reassembly with small debounce windows and showing partial replies. Also our SDK supports resume tokens so you can patch the UI without losing continuity.
[04:08] Omar: Resume tokens — is that safe for privacy? We don't want prompt leakage across sessions.
[04:15] Marcus: Resume tokens are opaque references — they don't contain plaintext. We also support per-tenant KMS encryption for cache blobs.
[04:23] Sofia: Any SOC2 or audit footprint on these blobs?
[04:27] Lara: Yes, we log cache pins and evictions in audit logs, and you can send those logs to your SIEM. We'll share the security brief after the call.
[04:36] Priya: Noted.
[04:40] Marcus: Now throwing a pathological case — 80k context with lots of unique tokens per session (low prefix reuse), ramp TPS to 300 for 2 minutes.
[05:00] Marcus: We already see per-token compute increasing and streaming starts to hit timeouts on long tails. Some client connections see a read timeout at around 18s if they expect continuous token streaming.
[05:12] Priya: 18s read timeout seems intolerable. Is that a Redwood timeout or client default?
[05:18] Marcus: That's client-side in this harness. Redwood runtime keeps working — tokens are generated but due to queueing and chunk assembly they aren't delivered before client read timeout. We recommend client retry with exponential backoff and chunk-idempotency to avoid duplication.
[05:32] Omar: But retrying could amplify the load, right?
[05:36] Marcus: Correct, naive retries exacerbate the problem. Our suggested pattern: short client timeout, then client checks the server for resume token or a small status endpoint to avoid re-submitting full work.
[05:48] Lara: Also note our fallback policy can route to a cheaper variant with reduced context depth to keep initial throughput — this preserves p50 while sacrificing some long-history fidelity. For Atlas's use case, you could route non-critical users to the cheaper path during spikes.
[06:02] Sofia: Can we have dynamic routing by account or by request header?
[06:06] Marcus: Yes — routing rules support headers, tokens, or even a feature flag. You can set canary percentages too.
[06:11] [15s pause, people typing] 
[06:30] Priya: Quick question — for your Dedicated setup, how many GPUs did you use in the test?
[06:36] Marcus: In Dedicated mode we provisioned an 8-GPU pool with reservation. That kept the KV cache warmer because memory is not shared with other tenants, and pinning allowed the 80k prefix to stay resident. p50 initial token latency dropped from 420ms to ~260ms in this configuration.
[06:55] Omar: That's promising. What about cost delta for Dedicated?
[06:59] Lara: We'll send a cost comparison. Short answer: Dedicated is higher OPEX but gives predictable p99 and reduces tail spikes. Optimize module can suggest quantization and batching settings to reduce cost for similar latency.
[07:12] Marcus: Jumping into telemetry — here's a chart (reference shared) showing latency vs context length. You'll see a knee at ~48k tokens where the kernel changes. Also watch memory pressure and GC-like pauses.
[07:29] Priya: The knee is concerning. Is there a compiler or kernel-level optimization you plan to add?
[07:34] Marcus: We're working on a fused attention path that keeps long-prefix memory references compact — ETA Q1 next year. Meanwhile, we recommend prefix pruning heuristics and delta-encoding repeated system messages.
[07:50] Sofia: Delta-encoding — does Redwood support automated prefix compression?
[07:54] Marcus: We provide a client-side library to canonicalize and compress repeated metadata, but full automatic compression is a roadmap item.
[08:05] Lara: Ok let's demo a fallback sequence. We'll intentionally saturate and then show how the system transitions through throttles, model fallbacks, and finally returns to normal. Marcus is toggling an injected failure mode now.
[08:20] Marcus: Injected failure: reduce worker concurrency by 40%.
[08:28] [simulated noise, queue metrics scroll] 
[08:33] Marcus: Immediately we see backlog growth, admission control tightens, and routing triggers fallback for heavy routes. Stream fragment frequency drops but we avoid catastrophic failures.
[08:46] Omar: What about client reconnections? We saw a reconnection thrash where mobile clients reopened socket frequently.
[08:52] Marcus: For mobile we recommend sticky sessions with resume tokens, and exponential reconnect jitter. Also set a client-side circuit-breaker so you don't thrash the network.
[09:02] Priya: Can the server side detect reconnection storms and apply mitigations?
[09:07] Marcus: Yes — server can apply rate limits per origin and escalate to temporary cold-fallback. We'll also put an adaptive token-bucket that deprioritizes noisy origins.
[09:19] Lara: Quick interlude — Priya asked about exportable telemetry. You get per-token latencies, per-request kernel path, cache hit/miss, and per-route error counts in the console. We'll share a sample export.
[09:34] Priya: Great. Can you also show us the console real quick for this run?
[09:39] Marcus: Switching screenshare — console shows live traces. Here you can filter by route and highlight the KV cache eviction events — see these sharp spikes? Those lines correspond to the 64k->80k cohorts.
[09:55] Sofia: I like the tracing but it's noisy. Can we get an aggregated alert rule for 'long history destabilization'?
[09:59] Marcus: Yes, you can set an alert on cache miss ratio + p99 latency. We'll include recommended thresholds in the playbook.
[10:10] [~10 minute run of additional stress cases — trimmed in this transcript] 
[20:15] Marcus: Mid-way note — when we increase chunk size from 512 to 1024, throughput improves slightly because fewer assembly operations, but memory pressure increases and cache churn goes up. There's a tradeoff.
[20:40] Priya: So what's your recommended starting point for Atlas?
[20:44] Marcus: For your mix (heavy histories + high burst TPS) start with chunk size 512, enable prefix pinning for VIP accounts in Dedicated, and set client timeout to 20s with resume token flow. Use Optimize to run a quantization pass — int8 gives you ~25% token CPU reduction for many models.
[20:58] Omar: About quantization — any model quality regressions at longer contexts?
[21:03] Marcus: Some models show small regression on tasks requiring very precise numeric coherence. Optimize can run a small A/B to quantify. Usually acceptable but test on your eval prompts.
[21:15] Lara: Let's discuss the pilot. We propose a 2-week Dedicated trial with a small reserved pool, Redwood runs two benchmark suites and Atlas shares representative datasets. Post-trial we'll have an ops review and possible commit.
[21:32] Priya: Timeline? We need results before holiday season.
[21:36] Lara: Start the trial next week if you can sign the trial SOW. That gives us two full weeks and an ops review the following Monday.
[21:45] Sofia: Who signs the SOW on your side?
[21:48] Lara: I'll send it, legal is on standby. Expected low-friction for trials.
[21:52] Omar: Any immediate gotchas we should know for our infra teams?
[21:56] Marcus: Ensure your VPC egress rules allow sustained bursts and avoid aggressive NLB timeouts; connection churn amplifies backpressure. Also give us IP ranges for ephemeral worker pools if you want whitelisting.
[22:09] Priya: Noted.
[22:12] Lara: Quick security note — audit logs and per-request metadata retention policies are configurable. We'll provide default 90-day retention but enterprise retention and deletion policies are customizable.
[22:26] [long pause while people scan docs] 
[22:55] Omar: Can we talk about observability costs? Exporting per-token telemetry seems expensive.
[23:02] Marcus: You can sample telemetry at route-level. For heavy routes sample at 1% for per-token, 100% for per-request aggregates. That keeps cost down while preserving signal.
[23:16] Priya: Do you have examples of other retailers that did similar Dedicated pilots?
[23:21] Lara: We'll anonymize but share a case study.
[23:26] Sofia: Are there any hard limits we should plan for? Like max context supported?
[23:31] Marcus: Currently we support up to ~100k tokens in terms of indexing and offload, but practical latency degrades beyond 80k without prefix reuse. We'll push on compiler optimizations to extend it.
[23:44] Priya: Understood.
[23:48] Lara: Let's summarize next steps and owners.
[23:52] Lara: Action items — I'll send SOW, pricing, and security brief. Marcus will run the requested 1M-sample TPS sim and provide logs. Priya to share eval dataset. Omar to coordinate VPC whitelisting.
[24:08] Priya: Sounds good. One more question — in the fallback to smaller model variant, how do you guarantee output consistency? We have downstream extractors tuned to the primary model's tokens.
[24:19] Marcus: Great point. We provide response normalization bridges—small adapters that translate certain output formats to a canonical schema. This reduces downstream drift during fallbacks.
[24:32] Sofia: If the fallback changes tokenization, can that break our parsers?
[24:36] Marcus: It can. That's why we recommend end-to-end tests in the pilot. Optimize can also run tokenization-drift checks.
[24:45] Lara: Ok final recap then.
[24:48] Lara: Pilot SOW sent by 2025-11-14, trial start target 2025-11-18, 2-week Dedicated reservation, Marcus to deliver 1M TPS sim results by 2025-11-20, Atlas to provide eval dataset by 2025-11-17. We'll follow with ops review and pricing review.
[25:10] Priya: Thanks all. Any last minute deep technical questions?
[25:15] Omar: None from me.
[25:16] Sofia: Good session, learned a lot.
[25:19] Lara: Great, we'll send notes. Thanks everyone.
[25:23] [call ends]
